title: Zen and Two Worlds Q&A
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of understanding and dialogue in addressing complex social issues, particularly when it comes to conflicts rooted in fundamentalist beliefs or extremist ideologies. Rather than resorting to force or simplistic solutions, Zoketsu Norman Fischer suggests that we should strive to comprehend the motivations behind such acts and engage with those who may be driven by these beliefs. By revisiting our traditional understanding of religion and embracing a more inclusive and compassionate approach, Buddhism can play a vital role in fostering tolerance, interfaith dialogue, and a more just society.

sentences.text: So, that was a long speech.
Sorry, I hope you are still with me.
Everybody seems to be still awake.
It's remarkable.
So maybe we could take a little time to talk about that, if you want to.
Does anybody have any comments or questions?
I hasten to say that when I write essays like this, I'm a little bit out of my depth, because I do a lot of meditation.
I chant.
I bow.
I hang out with my friends.
This doesn't make me an expert on society, religion, and history.
So if anybody has any correctives, things that I might have completely misconstrued, please let me know.
That will improve my essay.
And if it made you have some thoughts that matter to you, please express them.
Anybody?
So she said, how do you talk to a suicide bomber when they're bent on doing what they're doing?
Well, anybody here ever met a suicide bomber?
I never have.
Anybody?
So we don't really know, actually, what a suicide bomber is thinking, or what they're like, or what their motivation is.
We have no idea.
The only thing we know about it is, well, two things.
First of all, our wildest fears, and second of all, what we read in the paper.
Neither one of those is too accurate.
So I think what you're implying in your question, and I didn't mean to say that we don't prevent suicide bombers from bombing.
No.

When something like that happens, the first thing you say, if you're any kind of a responsible person, is that we should be doing everything that can possibly be done to prevent this from happening again.

While we're preserving some kind of decency and human rights, we should question people, we should arrest people, we should investigate, we should use our strength in whatever way we need to, to prevent this from happening, because this is terrible for everybody concerned.

So I don't mean to say that our defense against suicide bombers would be, in case a suicide bomber comes into the restaurant where we're having lunch, before they pull the cord on their bomb, we say, just a moment, we'd like to speak with you about what you're doing.
Let's talk about this.
I don't think that would be that workable.
But I think we're all pretty pushed around by our fear, by our confusion, and by our distortion of what we're reading in the newspaper and hearing on the radio.
We haven't really thought about what this all means.
We haven't talked to each other about it.

Certainly, wherever there are opportunities for dialogue with fundamentalist religious people of any stripe, we should have those dialogues, and we should take these people seriously, and find out where they're coming from, and who they are, and what motivates them, and what they're thinking.
Maybe there's something we're missing here.
I think we are missing something.
That's all I'm saying.

I remember, after 9-11, I was, of course, very upset, and I put on the Everyday Zen website, and I made flyers that I was distributing right and left saying that this is a tremendously awful thing that has happened, and we need to do three things.
First, we need to thoroughly grieve.
Second, we need to prevent this from ever happening again.
And third, we need to try to understand why this happened.
And this is not what our government, in my opinion, has done.
Therefore, I think by declaring war on terror, we have made a big, big mistake, I believe.
I don't say we shouldn't prevent terror, but it's like if your teenage child throws a tantrum, it is not the thing to do to say, from now on, we're at war, until you are different.
We are at war.
We are at war.
How would this work at home, folks?
Not that well.
You don't want that child to throw tantrums, and you're going to prevent that in whatever way you can, with strength, parental authority, and whatever strength you can muster.
But you don't declare war, because what does that do?
That ups the ante, that makes things worse.
You say to the child, why did you do that?
What's going on?
And that makes a big difference, if you respond that way, versus if you declare war.
So I didn't get elected president, so what do I know?
I don't know if that's a good idea.
I'm just telling you, that's what I feel, and that's what I felt.
And I was very disturbed when the president said, these people are evil.
Because I think what the meaning of that was, these people don't count, are not to be in any way seen as human beings.
They should be excised from the human family.
It's an understandable response to a horrible act like that, but it's not a policy.
Anyway, I apologize for getting on the soapbox, but that was your question.
Yeah.
Well, to me, what's different about the current situation is that I really believe there is a serious religious dimension to this that's going on.
In other words, I think it's different from political oppression.
There may be political dimensions to it, but I think that's a kind of political argument that social reform is needed and so on, economic reform.
But it is true, I think that is certainly true.
And we've seen that so many times before.
When people have no outlet to express themselves and no way to change things, in their desperation they take up arms.
It's happened over and over and over again.
I'm sorry, Freud, as what?
To assert my independence, you mean?
Yeah.
Did you all hear what he said?
No.

Well, he was basically saying, if I paraphrase, because I got the mic, that it may be that the reason people fight one another is not to harm one another or dominate one another, but simply to be seen as equals together, that that's the reason somebody maybe fights: to be acknowledged by the other.
I'm sure that's so in many, many cases, especially with these ethnic cases of one group in a country fighting another group.
It's often like that.

Well, I think that's similar to my point of view, that to understand that would be to have a much more intelligent approach to the situation, rather than just applying might without any attempt to understand.
Yes.
Yeah, please.
So you mean my personal feelings about Japanese Buddhism or my own spiritual practice?
I see.

Well, I'm not sure how to get a handle on your question, to be honest with you, but what occurs to me to say in response is that what I have found in my own life path, through my spiritual practice over all these years, in a very different way from the way it is for Japanese people, but in my own way, because I'm a westerner, an American, and so on, is that I have come to appreciate the liminal world and see its importance in my own life.

Well, the thing that I learned on the trip to Japan that I had forgotten, and I think I knew it before, but I forgot it, was that the Japanese also have this in their practice, but in a very different way.
So what I'm saying for all of us is that I believe we all need this.
We all need a religious dimension to our lives that is significant.
I think a lot of religion is not significant in that sense.
In other words, we might go to church or synagogue, feel part of an identity of a community, but we really don't have our souls turned inside out by our encounter with our religion.
It's just not that strong a factor in our lives for most people, with the exception of mostly people who have what we call fundamentalist beliefs.
Those people actually have had their lives turned inside out by that, and that's where they're coming from, and that's why they're looking at the rest of us and saying, you don't understand.
So I think we have to have a religious life, in my opinion, because I would say that, right?
Ask a doctor, he'll tell you you're sick.
But I actually believe it, that we all need a way, and it may be that our old understandings of what religions are and how they work need to be completely revised.

We may need to have a different way of doing religion and a different understanding of what it is, and each one of us may have a significant religious life that we can share with one another, even if we're doing it in different ways.
Because in a sense, that's what the Japanese have as a consequence of their long history.
There's a shared sense of meaning in the society that has to do with religion, even though they don't practice it, because it's so deeply ingrained in being Japanese, and we don't have that.
So we're exporting this secularism all over the world, and some people are freaking out.
Because I think, to be sure, there are two problems.
There's also social and economic injustice.
There's no question about that, because that's obvious, and we know that, and that needs to be changed, of course.
But I think there's also something else going on.
That's the part that I'm seeing.
So that's what I believe we all need to do for ourselves, each one of us for our own good, but also for the good of our civilization and our society.

If we think about it, if we figure out that what we've got to do is smash terrorists and create a society that is constantly at war with these other bad guys who might be anywhere, at any time, there might be a dozen suicide bombers sitting here in the audience.
I really don't know.
I mean, it's possible.
So I have to be eternally vigilant, and I have to search everybody who comes in the door, and we have to have a whole world like that.
If that's the solution to this, I don't know.
Did you hear what he said, that a lot of, to paraphrase, a lot of religious texts that he cited, the Dead Sea Scrolls, state in the text, exclusivity.
We've got the truth, everybody else is wrong.
So maybe we need a non-text-based religion.
Well, I think we need all kinds of religion.
We do need a non-text-based religion.
And how are we going to tell the people who want to have a text-based religion that they can't do that?
They can't do that.
But we can say, look, you're misunderstanding that text.
Jesus did not mean that you should smash the infidels.
He didn't mean that.
Neither did the prophet Mohammed.
That's not what they meant.
These people taught love.
They didn't teach exclusivity.
They didn't teach that everybody has to be Islamic or Protestant or Catholic in order to be loved, in order to be worthwhile.
They didn't teach that.
I don't accept that.
Let's talk about it.
Let's argue about it.
Let's debate it.
So I think all religious texts have, even those [unclear: "Debzis"] texts, benefit and teachings that are valuable.
And we have to learn how to read them.
I think people don't know how to read their own texts sometimes in their own religions.
That's my opinion.
Well, that's a great question.
It makes me think of what role Buddhism has in all this that I'm talking about.
And I think Buddhism actually has a possible, really important role to play in all this.
Because, for one thing, as a non-theistic religion, Buddhism doesn't propose, this is the God, this God dictates that you should live in this way.
Buddhism basically says, try this out.
This might help your life.
Here's a way of touching your heart at the deepest level.
And Buddhism, I think, has in many ways a kind of built-in tolerance, because it has that attitude.
So I think Buddhism can be very helpful in inter-religious dialogue.
I've done a lot of inter-religious dialogue in which I can see that the Buddhist point of view can help all of us to understand one another.
The other thing, too, is that a lot of Buddhist practices are, in a way, quite generic, like Zen meditation, where you sit and breathe and pay attention to your body.
There's nothing Buddhist about that, actually.

In fact, Tim mentioned in the beginning that I'm quite active in the Jewish meditation movement, and somewhat less active, but active, in the Christian meditation movement, in which Christians and Jews are using silent sitting meditation as a way of entering more deeply into their Christian or Jewish spirituality.
So Buddhism has that as a gift to offer to the other traditions, not in any way trying to get people to be Buddhists, but trying to give them another way.

And what we found in the Jewish meditation that's so interesting, and it goes to what you said, is that through meditation practice, people are now beginning to read their Bible differently, to see different things in it, because of their inner experience from the sittings.
I think that is something really valuable.
Buddhism, I think, is the only religion I know of where you really don't have to be a Buddhist to practice Buddhism.

In the Sangha that I have at home, for some reason, I don't know why this is, we have a whole Episcopalian group, a whole bunch of people who are church-going Episcopalians who are regular attenders of our group.
And it's kind of delightful.
There's no feeling that, well, you Episcopalians better straighten out here, you know what I mean?
We celebrate this.
We think this is great, and we're always asking and talking all the time about our religious experiences and so on.
This is what we need.
I think Buddhism has that capacity.
And so I'm yakking about all this stuff, right?
Here I am in front of all of you saying this, but you're right.
In general, most Buddhists are focused on their own groups and their own practice.

It's natural, of course, and most Buddhists are thinking, who are we in this big American religious world in which everybody's a Christian or this or that, and we're just here in our little living room sitting together?
We're nobody.

I think that as time goes on, I hope that Buddhists will realize that they're not trying to convert anybody or take over the world or this or that, but they should help the religious world to be more religious, in my view.
So maybe that'll happen someday.
But that's actually why I'm here tonight and why I'm saying the things I'm saying and why I'm writing an article for the Sun, because I'm trying.
It's slow, because it's very hard to make this case.
If you talk about religion, right away people think they know what religion is, and they like it or they don't like it, or they like your religion or they don't.
End of story.
It's hard to get through and say, no, religion isn't what you think it is.
There's a different way to understand it, and it's desperately needed that we understand it.
How can we possibly face, never mind the terrorism and all this problem, but the crisis of the planet, the atmosphere and global warming and all that, and all the things that are going to happen?
How in the world are we going to face those things without a religious point of view?
How can you possibly face it with, like, science?
Now, of course, science.
We've got to do things and study the question.
I'm not saying that it's irrelevant.
But that's not a point of view for the heart to understand and endure, and make meaning out of the things that are going to happen to us.
How are we going to understand those things and endure with clarity and compassion if we don't have religion?
And we can't have the kind of narrow-minded, let's-beat-each-other-up religion that we've had in the past.
We can't have that.
So we need a new kind of religion.
And I think Buddhism does have an important role to play now, in this time.
So that's, like I say, why I'm here.
I think probably that's a long night.
It is for me.
Thank you very much for coming.
I really hope that you'll think about these things and think about your own spiritual life.
And goodness knows, if you stumble into the Dharma Hall, the Bellingham Zen group and the other groups in the Dharma Hall will welcome you and will help you.
You'll find something helpful, I think.
So please do that if you have any inclination to do it.
This lecture series is an attempt, the first time.
It's really thanks to Tim that this is happening.
I've given a few little talks here and there, but publicly, this is the first attempt for Bellingham Buddhists to do what you're suggesting, to stand up and say, here we are.
We don't have all the answers.
We're not experts on everything.
But here we are and we want to help and we want to be part of this.
So, yeah, exactly.
It's wonderful.
That's right.

So please support the lecture series, because I hope that the lecture series can be a public forum for people from different religions and no religion to come together and discuss these things that matter so much to all of us.
So thanks for coming tonight.
We'll see you.
Take care of yourselves.
